answer.line: Both rings can close, but only this one keeps an H between the two carbonyls. Ethoxide takes it, and that locks the product in.

steps: Find the two alpha carbons: C2, a CH carrying the methyl, and C5, a CH2. Each can attack the ester at the other end.
Count both rings: each closes five atoms. The C5 enolate leaves a CH between ketone and ester; the C2 enolate leaves a carbon with no H at all.
Dieckmann is reversible until ethoxide pulls that doubly activated H, so a ring without one reopens and drains to the ring that has one. That is the favored ring.

choices.note: Same formula as the key, but the methyl carbon was counted into the ring. The chain closes five atoms, and the methyl stays outside.
The CH2 end attacks, the methyl rides beside the ketone, and an acidic H sits between the two carbonyls.
This is the product from plain diethyl adipate. Here the 2-methyl group has nowhere to go, so it has to show up on the ring.
This is one ring a 3-methyl diester could give. Here the methyl sits on an alpha carbon, so it ends up next to a carbonyl, not across the ring.
This ring does form. But its carbon between the carbonyls carries the methyl and no H, so ethoxide cannot lock it in, and it reverts.

lockIt: A Dieckmann ends where ethoxide can pull an H from between the two carbonyls.

playWith.label: Tree, the alpha carbon: pick ethyl acetate and the Claisen, the same ester enolate move a Dieckmann makes inside one chain

reactants.label: diethyl 2-methyladipate: C5 or C2 can attack

products.label: favored: an H left between the C=O groups
other closure: no H there, it reopens

visual.note: Both closures make five-membered rings. Ethoxide pulling the H between the carbonyls is the step that keeps one.
visual.reuse: SmilesDrawer through the light copy of tools/ochem/tree/draw.js
visual.alt: Diethyl 2-methyladipate, with its CH2 alpha carbon marked as the attacker, gives two possible five-membered rings with NaOEt. In the favored ring a marked acidic H sits on the carbon between the ketone and the ester; the other closure puts the methyl there, leaves no H, and reopens.
visual.caption: Look at the carbon between the two C=O groups in each ring. Only one still has an H.
